text: Eggs need 38–39°C and the right humidity to hatch; these conditions are also ideal for bacteria, so dirty eggs should not be incubated, and washing eggs is not recommended since it destroys their natural protective coating. A hen incubates by sitting on a clutch of 8 to 13 eggs almost full time, leaving the nest only about 15 minutes a day to eat lightly — she must be in good body condition before she starts setting. She turns the eggs regularly with her beak to keep the embryo from sticking to the shell and to provide a little oxygen. Incubation takes 21 days. Candling — shining a light through the egg, using an opening smaller than the egg's diameter — lets you check whether an egg is fertilized; after one week of incubation a correctly developing embryo shows as a web of vessels around a dark spot. Hatching can take 4 to 12 hours for the chick to break free of the shell. A newly hatched chick is wet and tired and will lie still for several hours before becoming dry, fluffy, and active. The yolk sac remaining in its body can sustain the chick for up to 48 hours.
